session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — what they eat, where they spend time, and who they spend it with. No academic or identity-political framing will be introduced. The collective identity is simply 'men talking about food and everyday life in the UK today', kept grounded and ordinary so participants feel safe speaking frankly rather than performing an identity or answering a thesis.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): The highest sensitivity area. Participants may default to 'no, gender doesn't affect what I eat' as a socially progressive performance, or conversely perform traditional masculinity. Behavioural grounding — specific situations, specific meals, specific social contexts — will be essential to get past the rehearsed answer.

Social context and judgment from peers: Across multiple sections, the role of other men's expectations and social judgment on what participants eat is likely to be underreported. Probing references to 'what mates would think' or embarrassment/pride around food will be important.

Plant-based shift (Sections 4 and 5): Risk of vague, hypothetical, or socially acceptable answers ('I'd need it to taste the same'). Need to push toward specific concrete barriers and real past moments — meals, occasions, relationships — not abstract preferences.

Consensus risk across the group: Five suburban British men in the 40–48 age bracket may converge quickly into a mutually reinforcing narrative (e.g., 'meat is normal, plant-based is fine but not for us'). Active dissent-inviting and sharpening moves will be needed if this hardens prematurely.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Unknown profile depth — suburban South East, 45. No specific signals. May lean toward considered, measured responses. Monitor for whether he defers to group consensus or holds independent positions.

48, East of England, suburban. Oldest in the group. May carry more settled food habits and be less likely to self-examine them. Watch for dismissiveness around gender framing — probe gently if he deflects.
45, South West, suburban. No specific signals. South West location may carry rural or outdoor-lifestyle associations worth noting if he references food in that context.

40, North West, suburban. Youngest in the group. May be slightly more open to challenging norms or may feel more self-conscious about expressing traditional views. Worth monitoring whether he adjusts his positions based on the room.
47, South East, suburban. Geographically similar to Andrew — watch for whether they form an informal alliance or echo chamber. No profile-specific signals beyond that.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender question: Men aged 40–48 are likely aware of public discourse around masculinity and may give progressive-sounding answers that don't reflect their actual behaviour or feelings. Use behavioural anchoring ('can you think of a specific time...') rather than attitude questions.

Rapid consensus on plant-based barriers: The group may quickly agree on taste, cost, or convenience as barriers to plant-based eating, producing shallow unanimity. Plan a sharpening hypothetical if this happens (e.g., 'what if taste and price were identical?').

Under-disclosure on peer judgment: Men are less likely to spontaneously name embarrassment or social pressure from peers as a food influence. This will need indirect probing — through situations, places, and social occasions — rather than direct questions about peer pressure.

Topic drift in Section 1 (male friendship/place): This section exists to warm up the group and surface social contexts. Risk of it becoming a travel log or pub-anecdote session. Keep it moving once a couple of good social contexts have emerged.

Potential early dominance: Without demographic differentiation, one or two participants may set a tone in Sections 1–2 that others then follow into Sections 3–5. Monitor and reactivate quieter voices before the main topic sections begin.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Very light touch. Let participants settle, find their voice, and build rapport. Minimal probing; warm, brief acknowledgements. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): Light to moderate — use it to surface concrete habits and social contexts that will be useful in later probing. Section 3 (gender and food): Push harder here. Use behavioural grounding early; challenge easy deflections; invite dissent if consensus forms. This is the section most likely to produce socially performed answers. Sections 4–5 (plant-based): Moderate to firm. Push past abstract barriers toward specific, lived moments. Use sharpening hypotheticals if the discussion stays at the level of generality. Section 6 (closing): Light. Let participants add anything unprompted, acknowledge the session genuinely, and close warmly without reopening exhausted threads.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive roughly 60% of total word budget combined, as they carry the core research questions. Context sections (1, 2) receive a moderate share — enough to surface meaningful material that will support later probing without becoming ends in themselves. Intro and closing sections receive the smallest shares. Section 3 receives the largest single allocation because it is the most sensitive and most likely to need probe depth and dissent management.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

group_has_agreed_easily_on: Suburban living as a preferred setup — space without being remote
Decompression time after work as a genuine need

last_engagement_round.hook: Nick's point about needing space to decompress but also not wanting to waste time commuting—that's hit on something I've definitely felt more acutely as I've gotten older. The balance shifts. Early on you don't mind the drive, but it does wear on you.

Nick's mention of the van commute between different sites resonates — I do similar work travelling across Norfolk and Suffolk. Also his point about having a young child and needing to decompress is something I can relate to in a different way, and it might be worth exploring what 'decompressing' actually means for people doing physical work versus office work.

Nick just mentioned having a young child and needing that decompression time — I've got grown kids now but remember that phase vividly. Also, he's the first one to mention family logistics beyond just the couple setup, and I relate to that juggling act of work travel and home life.

Nick just mentioned the balance between space and time at home since having a young child — that's something I can relate to even without kids. The work-from-home setup means I'm already home, but I've noticed how that changes what 'decompressing' actually means. It's not just about distance from work anymore.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was introductory: participants established themselves as suburban, working men (construction, logistics, electrical, HR, driving) spread across Norfolk, South East, and North West. A loose theme of suburban living as pragmatic balance emerged — space without isolation, manageable commutes, evening recovery time — with Nick and John briefly touching on how having young children sharpens awareness of time and the need to decompress after work.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening was deliberately low-stakes — name and location only — to ease participants in without pressure. Conversation flowed voluntarily and organically, with participants building on each other's comments unprompted, which is a positive sign for group dynamic. I held back entirely and let the thread develop naturally. The transition into the first substantive question was clean. No intervention was needed, and none was made.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, welcome and thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. I'm the moderator for this session. We've got about 45 minutes together, and the whole thing will be recorded for research purposes, so just bear that in mind. Before we get going, a couple of quick things: there are no right or wrong answers here — genuinely, I'm not looking for any particular response, and I'm not going to be jumping in to agree or disagree with what you say. What matters is what you actually think and what you've actually experienced, not what sounds like the right thing to say. It's also meant to be a conversation, so if someone says something that connects with your experience, or you want to push back on something, please just jump in — you don't have to wait to be asked. And equally, if something doesn't apply to you, that's fine to say too. Try not to overthink it — just speak as you would normally. Okay, let's get started. Why don't we go around briefly and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.

I'm Daniel. I'm from just outside Norwich, in Norfolk — suburban area, East of England. Been there a good while now with my wife. I work in construction, so I'm out on sites most days across the region, but that's where I'm based.

Right, yeah — I'm Paul, I'm down in the South East, suburban area as well. Not too far from London actually, bit further out though. I work from home mostly, so I'm not out on sites like you Daniel, but I do know the region pretty well. I'm in HR and training, so quite different work to construction, but yeah — I get what you mean about the suburban setup. My wife and I have been in our place a good few years now. It's nice having that bit of space without being right in the thick of things, you know?

Right, yeah, I'm Andrew. South East as well, suburban — so I'm kind of in that same boat as you two really. I work in logistics, so transport and warehousing, bit more on the management side of things now. Commute into work most days, so I'm not home-based like Paul, but I know exactly what you mean about the space thing. That's actually one of the reasons I've stayed put where I am. You get enough room to breathe without being stuck in the middle of everything, you know? And honestly, for the work I do — early starts, that kind of thing — having a bit of distance but not being hours away works well. You can get home and actually have an evening to yourself.

Right, yeah — Nick, from the North West actually. I'm based just outside Manchester, suburban area. I work in electrical installation, so I'm out on jobs pretty much every day, moving between different sites — houses, offices, that sort of thing. So a bit like you Daniel with the travel, but it's usually shorter distances, customer premises rather than big construction sites.

I get what you're saying about the space and distance thing though, Andrew. That's pretty much where I am too. I've got a mortgage on a semi near me, wife's working full-time as well, and we've got a little one under five, so it's... yeah, it works having a bit of room but not being miles from anywhere. The commute thing's a bit different for me since I'm not going to the same place every day — I'm just driving between jobs in the van — but I know what you mean about wanting an actual evening when you get back. That's the thing I've noticed more since we've had the kid, to be honest. You need that bit of space to decompress, but you also can't afford to be spending two hours in the car when you could be at home.

Yeah, Nick, I hear that. I remember when my kids were that age — under five — it's relentless, isn't it? You come home knackered from work and you've still got to be present for them, help with bedtime, all that. I was doing long hours back then too, driving for work, and some nights I'd be back late and just... done. But you can't be done, can you? Not when there's a little one waiting.

The decompression thing you're talking about — that's real. Even now, after a long shift, I just need twenty minutes with the radio or the telly before I can actually be around people properly. But with a young kid, you don't really get that luxury. You're straight into it.

I've got a bit of space here at home now, which helps. Just the two of us, so if I need to tinker with the van or just sit outside for a bit, nobody's needing anything. But I remember the days when that wasn't an option, and yeah — having that suburb setup where you're not sitting in traffic for hours trying to get back was important. Otherwise you'd lose the whole evening.

Thanks John — and good to have everyone on board. Right, let's get into it. Thinking about where you actually spend time with your male friends — what's your favourite kind of place for that? Could be somewhere specific, could be a type of place. Why that one?
